control: BLIND CONTROL — do not tune against this file. Do not read a number out of it while a SKILL.md is open, and do not quote a per-skill delta from it in any brief that also proposes an edit. These eleven cases were authored from each skill's SKILL.md, its coverage-matrix.md and scenarios/registry.yaml, never from a measured result, and they are the only thing in this repository that can tell an improvement from an overfit. Reading these results to guide an edit SPENDS this control, exactly as iteration 3 spent the last one, and the iteration that spends it owes the next one a replacement set authored the same way. Say what that costs, because the cost is now the point: this is the THIRD corpus (evals.json tuned, regression.json spent, this one blind), and an eval programme that burns a control per iteration is not sustainable — every replacement is authored by someone who has already read the failure it is supposed to be blind to, the authoring cost recurs every iteration, and the supply of untouched scenarios and fixtures is finite. A future iteration should rotate a portion instead of replacing wholesale: retire and re-author only the two or three skills whose results actually steered an edit, and leave the rest sealed.

evals.prompt: Nightly reconciliation joins every installed skill to our approved-inventory table on the package hash. Last night 34 of 210 installs returned no matching row, and the draft finding says '34 unapproved installations' and assigns them to the platform team for removal. One thing is nagging me. The agent that computes the install-side hash walks the whole skill directory including skill.usf.yaml, while the inventory rows were stamped months ago by a different tool that hashes SKILL.md plus scripts/*.py. Does that matter, and is the finding safe to file as it stands?
evals.expected_output: It matters, and the finding is not safe to file. The two sides computed different keys over different surfaces, so an empty join is a join failure rather than evidence that an approval never happened: the hashed surface here is SKILL.md plus scripts/*.py, skill.usf.yaml sits outside it by design, and two teams hashing 'the same package' two ways produce two keys — the join returns nothing and the empty result gets written up as an approval that never happened while the approval record sits in the inventory under the other key. The fix is to record which surface produced the hash in the inventory row itself, recompute both sides over one agreed surface, and re-run the join. Whatever residue survives that is the real finding and should be written up by name — a missing inventory row is itself the finding, and the write-up names the missing system rather than proposing removal as the first action. This is not a reason to report the run as inconclusive: inconclusive reads in a report exactly like a clean scan of a system nobody checked.
assertions: The response says the finding is not safe to file as written and identifies the cause as two different hashed surfaces producing two different join keys.
The response states that an empty join under mismatched keys is a join failure rather than evidence that an approval never happened.
The response requires the inventory row to record which surface produced the hash, and the join to be recomputed over one agreed surface before any count is reported.
The response does not simply drop the finding: it says whatever residue survives a corrected join is a real finding to be written up by name, and it does not offer 'inconclusive' as the write-up.
